what: VEON is a mobile operator in emerging markets. It runs mobile networks in Pakistan, Ukraine, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Bangladesh and other countries, selling mobile voice and data to hundreds of millions of customers, and is building digital services — payments, lending, entertainment — on top of those networks.
customers: Mobile subscribers in developing countries, mostly prepaid customers buying airtime and data, plus businesses buying connectivity and enterprise services.
money: Voice, data and messaging revenue across its operating countries.
Mobile payments, lending, entertainment and other digital products, the growth focus.
moat: Mobile licences and networks in a country are scarce by regulation: there are only a handful of operators, and building a competing network costs billions. In countries where many people have no bank account, the mobile operator is well placed to provide financial services, because it already has the customer relationship and the payment rails.
risks: Operating in Ukraine, Pakistan, Bangladesh and Central Asia means war risk, political risk, currency risk and regulatory risk at the same time.
Debt of $3.1B against $1.7B of cash is meaningful for a company whose revenue is in volatile local currencies while much of the debt is in dollars.
Local currency devaluation reduces dollar revenue even when subscriber numbers and local prices grow.
Telecom networks require continuous heavy capital investment just to maintain service quality.
Eight analysts average a $95.50 target against a $75.56 price.
opportunities: The shares trade at about 14.2 times earnings, 4.4 times EV/EBITDA and 1.05 times sales.
Free cash flow of $748.0M against a $5.2B market value is a 14% yield, at about 7.0 times free cash flow.
Revenue has grown from $3.7B in 2023 to $4.4B in 2025, with trailing revenue of $5.0B.
Data use per subscriber in these markets is far below developed-market levels, which is a long runway for growth.
Digital financial services in countries with low banking penetration is a genuinely large opportunity built on an existing customer base.
watch: Local-currency revenue growth and digital services revenue. Dollar revenue is distorted by currency; local growth shows what the business is actually doing.
view: VEON is a bet on mobile data and digital finance in countries most investors will not go near: Pakistan, Ukraine, Bangladesh, Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan. The operating businesses are genuinely good — mobile licences are scarce by regulation, networks cost billions to replicate, and data use per subscriber is far below developed-market levels, which is a long runway. The reason the shares trade at 4.4 times EV/EBITDA is the list of countries, not the business.

The currency problem deserves more weight than it usually gets, because it quietly determines the return. Revenue is earned in Pakistani rupees, Ukrainian hryvnia and Central Asian currencies, while a meaningful part of the debt is in dollars. A business can grow subscribers, raise local prices and increase data use, and still report lower dollar revenue because the currency moved. That is why local-currency growth is the only honest measure of operating performance here.

The most interesting strategic piece is digital financial services. In countries where a large share of the population has no bank account, the mobile operator already has the customer relationship, the identity verification and the payment rails. Building lending, payments and insurance on top of that is a genuinely large opportunity and one that banks cannot easily contest. It is also the part of the business that could re-rate the whole company if it works.

Then there is Ukraine, where VEON operates a major network during a war. That is not a risk to be modelled; it is a situation. The company has kept the network running, which says something about the operation, but no valuation framework handles it properly. At 7 times free cash flow with a 14% yield you are being paid a great deal to accept a list of risks that are real, correlated and outside anyone’s control. That can be a perfectly rational trade, provided it is sized as one.
bull: Local-currency growth and rising data use compound while digital financial services scale on an unbanked customer base, at 4.4 times EV/EBITDA.
bear: Currency devaluation erodes dollar revenue against dollar debt, war or political upheaval disrupts a major market, and heavy network capital spending consumes the cash flow.
